questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure network access policies by using Azure Virtual Network Manager
questions.prompt: A central team needs a rule denying inbound RDP from the internet that no application team can override with their own NSG. Which action on a Virtual Network Manager security admin rule achieves this?
options: Allow, because it takes precedence over NSG rules
AlwaysAllow, because it stops further evaluation
Deny, because no NSG can permit traffic an admin rule has denied
Any action, because admin rules always override NSGs
questions.explanation: Security admin rules are evaluated before NSGs. Deny blocks and stops evaluation, so the NSG never runs. Allow permits evaluation to continue, meaning an NSG can still deny. AlwaysAllow stops evaluation in the other direction - use it for traffic that must survive an over-broad local deny.
why_not: Allow lets evaluation continue to the NSG, which can still decide the outcome - including permitting RDP.
AlwaysAllow ends evaluation by guaranteeing traffic is permitted - the opposite of the requirement.
Only Deny and AlwaysAllow end evaluation. Allow hands the decision to the NSG.
questions.scenario_clue: "no application team can override with their own NSG" and the goal is to block - a Deny admin rule blocks the traffic before any NSG is evaluated. AlwaysAllow is final too, but it allows; Allow leaves the decision to the NSGs.
questions.misconception: Any security admin rule action overrides NSGs

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure network access policies by using Azure Virtual Network Manager
questions.prompt: A security admin configuration is saved with the correct rules targeting the correct network group, and has no effect on any virtual network. What is missing?
options: The rule collection priority is above 4096
The configuration was never deployed to a region
The network group uses static rather than dynamic membership
The virtual networks lack an NSG for the admin rules to override
questions.explanation: Nothing takes effect until you deploy the configuration to the regions in use. A saved-but-undeployed configuration produces no enforcement, no error and no clue in the rule view, which makes it the classic 'why isn't my rule working' answer.
why_not: Rule priority orders rules within a configuration that is in force. It cannot explain a configuration having no effect at all.
Static and dynamic membership only change how virtual networks join the group. With the right members, either works.
Security admin rules do not need an NSG to exist. They are evaluated whether or not one is present.
questions.scenario_clue: "saved ... and has no effect" - Virtual Network Manager configurations do nothing until they are deployed to target regions.
questions.misconception: Saving a Virtual Network Manager configuration applies it

questions.sub_skill: Implement and manage network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
questions.prompt: A NIC has an NSG allowing TCP 443 inbound at priority 200 and denying it at priority 150. The subnet NSG allows 443 at priority 100. Does traffic on 443 reach the VM?
options: Yes - the subnet NSG allows it and subnet rules take precedence
Yes - the lowest priority number across both NSGs wins
No - traffic must pass both NSGs, and the NIC NSG denies at 150 before reaching 200
No - NSGs are stateless, so a matching outbound rule is also required
questions.explanation: Inbound traffic is evaluated against the subnet NSG first, then the NIC NSG, and must pass both. Within the NIC NSG, first match wins and 150 is evaluated before 200. NSGs are stateful, so no outbound rule is needed for return traffic.
why_not: Subnet rules do not take precedence. Inbound traffic must pass the subnet NSG and then the NIC NSG.
Priority numbers are compared only within one NSG. Each NSG is evaluated on its own, and both must allow.
NSGs are stateful, so return traffic needs no outbound rule.
questions.scenario_clue: "NIC has an NSG" and "subnet NSG" - inbound traffic must pass both, and inside the NIC NSG the lower priority number (150, deny) is matched first.
questions.misconception: The lowest priority number across both NSGs decides the outcome

questions.sub_skill: Implement and manage network security groups (NSGs) and application security groups (ASGs)
questions.prompt: You need flow-level logging for traffic allowed and denied across your virtual networks. What should you configure?
options: NSG flow logs, with traffic analytics enabled
Virtual network flow logs
Diagnostic settings on each network security group
Connection monitor in Network Watcher
questions.explanation: NSG flow logs cannot be created - new ones have been unavailable since 30 June 2025 - and the feature retires on 30 September 2027. Virtual network flow logs replace them, and they are also the only place traffic allowed or denied by Virtual Network Manager security admin rules is visible.
why_not: New NSG flow logs cannot be created since 30 June 2025, and the feature retires on 30 September 2027.
Diagnostic settings on an NSG do not produce flow-level records. Flow logging is a Network Watcher feature, and virtual network flow logs are its current form.
Connection monitor tests reachability between endpoints. It does not log the flows passing through your networks.
questions.scenario_clue: "flow-level logging" across virtual networks - virtual network flow logs replace NSG flow logs, which can no longer be newly created.
questions.misconception: NSG flow logs are still the way to log network flows

questions.sub_skill: Implement and configure security for virtual private network (VPN) connections
questions.prompt: Remote users connecting over point-to-site VPN must be subject to Conditional Access and MFA. Which configuration is required?
options: IKEv2 with certificate authentication
SSTP with RADIUS authentication
OpenVPN with Microsoft Entra ID authentication
Any tunnel type, with Entra ID authentication selected
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID authentication for point-to-site requires the OpenVPN tunnel type. IKEv2 and SSTP support certificate and RADIUS authentication only, neither of which brings the connection under Conditional Access.
why_not: IKEv2 supports certificate and RADIUS authentication only, neither of which brings the connection under Conditional Access.
SSTP supports certificate and RADIUS authentication only. Entra ID authentication needs OpenVPN.
Entra ID authentication is available only with the OpenVPN tunnel type.
questions.scenario_clue: "Conditional Access and MFA" for point-to-site - Entra ID authentication for VPN requires the OpenVPN tunnel type.
questions.misconception: Entra ID authentication works with any point-to-site tunnel type

questions.sub_skill: Configure security for an Azure Virtual WAN
questions.prompt: Your Virtual WAN hub connects spoke virtual networks and branch offices. Traffic between any two spokes, and between branches and spokes, must be inspected by Azure Firewall in the hub. Internet-bound traffic must also be inspected, and must then leave through the on-premises default route rather than directly from Azure. What should you configure?
options: Deploy Azure Firewall in the hub, configure routing intent with a private routing policy, add 0.0.0.0/0 to its additional prefixes, and configure no internet routing policy
Deploy Azure Firewall in the hub, and configure routing intent with a private routing policy and an internet routing policy
Deploy Azure Firewall in the hub, and configure routing intent with only an internet routing policy
Deploy Azure Firewall in the hub, and add a user-defined route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall on every spoke subnet
questions.explanation: A secured virtual hub inspects what routing intent sends through it. The private routing policy covers traffic between virtual networks, branches and ExpressRoute. Forced Tunnel - inspect internet traffic, then send it on through a 0.0.0.0/0 route learnt from on-premises - is built from that private policy: add 0.0.0.0/0 to its additional prefixes and configure no internet routing policy. If no 0.0.0.0/0 route is learnt, internet traffic does not reach on-premises: Azure Firewall without a public IP drops it, and with one it leaves through that IP.
why_not: An internet routing policy always means Direct Access: internet traffic is inspected and then leaves straight from Azure, not through on-premises. The portal will not even add an internet policy to a hub in Forced Tunnel mode.

Without a private routing policy, traffic between spokes and between branches and spokes is not sent through the firewall - and an internet routing policy is Direct Access, so internet traffic would not go through on-premises either.

Spoke route tables only affect traffic leaving the spokes. They do not bring branch traffic through the firewall or send internet traffic via on-premises; routing intent is the hub's own mechanism for both.
questions.concept: Secured virtual hub and routing intent
questions.misconception: Sending internet traffic out through on-premises needs an internet routing policy
questions.scenario_clue: "between spokes, and between branches and spokes" = a private routing policy; "leave through the on-premises default route" = Forced Tunnel, which is that private policy plus 0.0.0.0/0 in additional prefixes, with no internet policy.
